title: Rien: The Revolution Seen from Every Window
subtitle: The French Revolution: Paris, Versailles and the provinces, 1789–1794
intro: On 14 July 1789 the king of France wrote one word in his journal, and it was 'nothing'. The word meant only that he had not hunted. That gap between the page and the street is the theme of this chapter. The Revolution was made in the gaps: between Versailles and Paris, between rumour and event, and between what a visitor felt in May and what he wrote in September.

The first cluster is July 1789. Arthur Young listens to orators in the Palais-Royal, then rides east and watches Strasbourg's town hall gutted. The Paris bookseller Hardy logs alarm bells and heads on pikes as reports reach his shop. A Norwich doctor, Edward Rigby, sees the heads of de Launay and Flesselles go by. On the 22nd Gouverneur Morris is waiting for his carriage when Foulon's head arrives. The same evening Jefferson sends Madison an account of a victory, with the killing in a postscript.

Then the royal family's own pages: Louis's flat log of 5 and 6 October 1789 and of Varennes, his sister Élisabeth's sharp letters, and his daughter's later memoir of disguises, the reporters' box on 10 August 1792, and the last supper in the Temple. Against them stand Rosalie Jullien, a republican mother cheering the guns of 10 August, and Restif de la Bretonne, roaming the September nights with a novelist's licence.

The execution of 21 January 1793 is seen at close range by the valet Cléry and the confessor Edgeworth, both writing later and both royalists. The best-placed foreign diarist in Paris, Morris, kept a diary from March 1789 to 1816, and it breaks off on 5 January 1793. It resumes only after he left Paris in October 1794. That silence is itself evidence of what keeping a diary under the Terror could cost.

The English radicals close the chapter. Helen Maria Williams fell in love with the Revolution at the Federation of 1790 and met it again from inside a prison. Mary Wollstonecraft watched the king ride to his trial and found herself in tears. The queen's last letter, never delivered, is the final dated page.
Read together, these eyes do not agree, and they are not meant to. They show how a revolution looks from the throne, the shop counter, the salon window, the roads of the provinces and the scaffold.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. From October 1793 the Republic used the Revolutionary calendar (Year I from 22 September 1792), so documents of the Terror may be dated by décadi, Prairial, Thermidor and so on. The Law of 22 Prairial Year II is 10 June 1794, and 9 Thermidor Year II is 27 July 1794. Entries here are converted to Gregorian dates.

eyes.name: Louis XVI
eyes.where: Versailles, then the Tuileries, then the Temple prison
eyes.authenticity: Autograph journal kept from 1766; a terse log of hunts, game killed, travel and ceremonies, not a diary of thoughts. Held at the Archives nationales (Musée des Archives, armoire de fer). Published by L. Nicolardot (1873). 'Rien' means 'no hunt / nothing killed', not 'nothing happened'.
eyes.bio: A king who recorded his life as a sportsman's tally. His one-word entry for 14 July 1789 became the most famous misreading in French history; read rightly, it shows how little of Paris reached the page of the man it was about.

sources.title: From the Archives: The Iron Closet (visit to the journal in the armoire de fer)
Armoire de fer (Wikipedia)
Louis XVI (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Siméon-Prosper Hardy
eyes.where: his shop and the streets around rue Saint-Jacques, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: same city, hearing and seeing the street
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript journal 'Mes loisirs, ou journal d'événemens tels qu'ils parviennent à ma connoissance', 1753–October 1789, eight manuscript volumes (BnF). A full critical edition is being published by Pascal Bastien, Sabine Juratic and Daniel Roche (Hermann, 2012– ). Entry contents below are summarised from the standard historiography, not checked line by line against that edition.
eyes.bio: For 36 years Hardy noted rumours, bread prices, executions and placards as they 'reached his knowledge'. His journal stops in October 1789, so it catches the old Paris giving way to the new and then goes silent.

sources.title: Siméon-Prosper Hardy (Wikipedia)
Mes loisirs (1753–1789), catalogue record

eyes.name: Gouverneur Morris
eyes.role: American businessman in Paris, aged 37; from 1792 United States Minister to France
eyes.where: Paris salons, the Palais-Royal, Versailles; his house in Paris through the Terror
eyes.authenticity: Autograph diary, 13 volumes, Library of Congress (1 March 1789–1816). There is a gap from 5 January 1793 to 12 October 1794, so the diary is silent on the king's execution and the Terror, which survive only in his letters. The 1888 edition by Anne Cary Morris is selective and tidied; Davenport's 1939 edition is fuller; the University of Virginia's digital edition corrects it.
eyes.bio: A one-legged New York patrician and womaniser who dined with ministers and wrote with dry wit. He was the only foreign minister to stay in Paris through the Terror, which makes his diary's silence from January 1793 all the more telling.

sources.title: The diary and letters of Gouverneur Morris, ed. A. C. Morris (1888), HathiTrust
Gouverneur Morris Papers, Library of Congress finding aid
The Diaries of Gouverneur Morris: Digital Edition (UVA Press)
Journal de Gouverneur Morris (Plon, 1901), Internet Archive

eyes.name: Thomas Jefferson
eyes.role: United States Minister to France, aged 46
eyes.authenticity: Letter-press copies and recipients' copies, published in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson (Princeton) and Founders Online. Fully authentic and dated.
eyes.bio: Jefferson wrote home almost daily through July 1789 and left Paris for good on 26 September. His tone is calmer and more hopeful than Morris's: he saw the killings as unfortunate exceptions in a just cause.

sources.title: Jefferson to Thomas Paine, 23 July 1789 (Founders Online)
Jefferson to James Madison, 22 July 1789 (Founders Online)

eyes.name: Arthur Young
eyes.role: English agricultural writer touring France on horseback, aged 48
eyes.where: Paris in June and early July 1789, then the roads of Lorraine, Alsace and Franche-Comté
eyes.authenticity: Day-dated travel journal, revised by Young for publication in 1792; the dates are generally trusted, but the wording is a reworked text and not a raw notebook.
eyes.bio: Young was counting soils and prices when the Revolution overtook him. His journal shows the provinces of 1789: hunger, rumour, châteaux burning, and an Englishman ordered to wear a cockade.

sources.title: Arthur Young's Travels in France, ed. Betham-Edwards (1909), HathiTrust
Voyages en France (French translation), Project Gutenberg
Travels in France (LibriVox audio)
Archives d'Alsace: the pillage of 20 July 1789 (notes Young's presence)

eyes.name: Edward Rigby
eyes.role: Norwich physician on a tour of the Continent, aged 42
eyes.where: the streets of Paris on and after 14 July 1789
eyes.authenticity: Letters home to his family, published by his daughter Lady Eastlake as 'Dr. Rigby's Letters from France &c. in 1789' (1880). Cited as an eyewitness source on the Bastille. The exact date of each letter was not checked here.
eyes.bio: Rigby walked into the crowds on the day of the Bastille and saw two heads go by on pikes. He began elated by the people's joy and ended shaken: a provincial doctor's view of the first revolutionary killings.

sources.title: Storming of the Bastille (Wikipedia; cites Rigby's letters)

eyes.name: Marc-Marie, Marquis de Bombelles
eyes.role: French ambassador to Venice, aged 45; a devout royalist
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript journal kept 1780–1822, published in full by Droz (Geneva, 1978–2013). The entry below is given only as a month-range and was not checked against the edition.
eyes.bio: A career diplomat whose wife, Angélique, was Madame Élisabeth's closest friend and correspondent. He shows the Revolution as it reached a royalist abroad: by courier and late, and taken as a personal disaster.

eyes.name: Madame Élisabeth (Élisabeth of France)
eyes.role: the king's youngest sister, aged 25 in 1789
eyes.where: Versailles, the Tuileries, the Varennes coach, the Temple
eyes.authenticity: Large surviving correspondence, mainly with Angélique de Bombelles and her exiled brothers; published in the 19th century (Feuillet de Conches edition, 1868, which contains some doubtful items). Treat individual letters with care.
eyes.bio: She refused to emigrate and shared every stage of her brother's fall. She was guillotined on 10 May 1794. Her letters are freer and sharper than anything the king wrote.

sources.title: Élisabeth of France (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Marie-Thérèse-Charlotte, Madame Royale
eyes.role: the king's daughter, aged 12 at Varennes and 14 at his death
eyes.where: the Varennes coach; the Tuileries; the Temple tower
eyes.authenticity: Her account of the flight to Varennes and her memoir of the Temple captivity were written later (the Temple memoir largely while she was still a prisoner, about 1795) from an autograph manuscript; an English translation by J. W. Croker appeared in 1823. It is not a day-by-day diary.
eyes.bio: She was the only member of the family in the Temple to survive. She was released on 18 December 1795. Her account gives the child's-eye view: the disguises, the silences, the last supper with her father.

sources.title: Marie-Thérèse of France (Wikipedia)
Princess Marie-Thérèse's journal of the flight to Varennes (Alpha History)

eyes.name: Jean-Baptiste Cléry
eyes.role: valet de chambre to the king in the Temple, aged 33
eyes.authenticity: 'Journal de ce qui s'est passé à la tour du Temple', published in London in 1798. It is set out like a journal but was written up after the events. The Directory had a spurious, distorted edition printed to undercut it, so use the London text.
eyes.bio: Cléry dressed, fed and read with the king for five months and woke him at 5 a.m. on 21 January 1793. His book became a royalist bestseller, and that is a reason to read it critically.

sources.title: Jean-Baptiste Cléry (Wikipedia)
Execution of Louis XVI (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Henry Essex Edgeworth de Firmont
eyes.role: Irish-born Catholic priest, the king's confessor, aged 47
eyes.where: the Temple, the carriage, and the scaffold steps
eyes.authenticity: Memoirs edited by C. S. Edgeworth, London 1815; French edition 1816. Written well after the event. The famous 'Fils de Saint Louis, montez au ciel' is traditional; Edgeworth himself neither confirmed nor denied saying it.
eyes.bio: An Irishman from Edgeworthstown who stood beside the king when the blade fell. He saw the final minutes at closer range than anyone else who left an account.

sources.title: Henry Essex Edgeworth (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Rosalie Ducrollay Jullien
eyes.role: wife of the deputy Marc-Antoine Jullien de la Drôme, aged 47
eyes.where: her lodgings in Paris, writing to her husband
eyes.authenticity: About 1,000 letters survive (Archives nationales). A selection was published by É. Lockroy as 'Journal d'une bourgeoise pendant la Révolution' (1881) with silent edits. Lindsay Parker's 'Writing the Revolution' (2013) works from the manuscripts. The entry below is dated approximately.
eyes.bio: A fervent, well-read republican mother who reported the streets to her absent husband like a war correspondent. She offers a woman's revolutionary enthusiasm, without the horror of the foreign visitors.

eyes.name: Nicolas Ruault
eyes.role: Paris bookseller and publisher, aged about 50
eyes.authenticity: Letters to his brother in Normandy, 1783–1796, published as 'Gazette d'un Parisien sous la Révolution' (ed. A. Vassal and C. Monnier, 1976). The dating of the entry below was not checked.
eyes.bio: A bookseller like Hardy who picks up where Hardy's journal stops. His letters move from patriotic hope to private dread as the Terror tightens.

eyes.name: Nicolas-Edme Restif de la Bretonne
eyes.role: novelist and printer, aged 58, a compulsive night-walker
eyes.where: the night streets near the prisons
eyes.authenticity: 'Les Nuits de Paris', with revolutionary instalments printed in 1793–94. It is a literary first-person work that mixes observation with invention, so treat it as testimony with a novelist's licence and not as a diary.
eyes.bio: Restif turned his insomnia into literature. His pages on the September massacres claim to see the Princesse de Lamballe's death up close, and they are as vivid as they are unreliable.

sources.title: Retif describes the September Massacres (Alpha History)

eyes.name: Helen Maria Williams
eyes.role: English poet, aged 30, who settled in Paris
eyes.where: the Champ de Mars in 1790; her Paris salon; the Luxembourg prison in 1793
eyes.authenticity: 'Letters Written in France' (1790) and later series (1792–96). These are open letters written for publication, sometimes dated only loosely. The dates below are approximate.
eyes.bio: She came to Paris for the Festival of the Federation and stayed, and she was imprisoned as a British subject in the Terror. Her letters are the radical English romance of the Revolution, written by someone who later knew its prisons.

eyes.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
eyes.role: English writer, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, aged 33
eyes.where: lodgings in the Marais, Paris, from December 1792
eyes.vantage_label: foreign radical in the same city
eyes.authenticity: Letters to her publisher Joseph Johnson, published by Godwin in 'Posthumous Works' (1798). The wording and dates are standard but were not re-checked here.
eyes.bio: She arrived in Paris to see the Revolution complete itself and instead watched its king driven to trial. Her letters show a defender of the Revolution shaken by what it was doing.

eyes.name: Marie Antoinette
eyes.role: Queen of France, aged 37 at her death
eyes.authenticity: Autograph last letter to Madame Élisabeth, 16 October 1793. It never reached her; it was found among Robespierre's or Courtois's papers and is now in the Archives nationales.
eyes.bio: She appears here only once, at the very end, in a letter written a few hours before the cart came for her.

sources.title: Marie Antoinette (Wikipedia)

entries.place: Versailles, a window at Mme de Flahaut's
entries.headline: The Estates-General procession: cheers for the king, silence for the queen
entries.digest: Morris watches the deputies process through Versailles from a friend's window. He notes that the crowd cheers Louis but gives the queen nothing, and he files the coldness away as a political fact.
entries.source_note: Journal de Gouverneur Morris (Plon 1901), entry 4 May 1789, Internet Archive PDF

entries.headline: An American republican moved to tears by a king's speech
entries.digest: At the opening session Morris finds himself weeping at the king's address. He again notes that the queen receives no public acclaim. The pageant still looks like a monarchy reforming itself, not one about to fall.
entries.source_note: Journal de Gouverneur Morris (Plon 1901), entry 5 May 1789

entries.headline: Pamphlets everywhere, and the court says nothing
entries.digest: Young finds the Palais-Royal coffee houses crowded to the doors, with people listening at the windows to orators. Pamphlets for liberty and against clergy and nobles pour out to the provinces. He is astonished that the court neither answers them nor stops them.
entries.source_note: Travels in France, entry 9 July 1789 (excerpt via Alpha History)

entries.place: on the road in Lorraine, walking a hill
entries.headline: A peasant woman's dues and taxes, on the day Paris rises
entries.digest: Walking his mare up a hill, Young falls in with a poor woman who lists what she owes a lord in wheat, chickens and oats, besides the king's taxes, with seven children to feed. She has heard that 'great people' mean to help the poor. While Paris erupts that same Sunday over Necker's dismissal, his page shows the grievance that lay under it.
entries.source_note: Travels in France, entry 12 July 1789 (Alpha History excerpt)

entries.headline: The king's log for the day of the Bastille
entries.digest: Louis's journal records no hunt for the day: the entry is a single word. He was not told of the fall of the Bastille until the next morning, when the Duc de La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt reportedly told him it was not a revolt but a revolution. The word measures the distance between Versailles and Paris, not the king's indifference.
entries.source_note: Journal of Louis XVI, 14 July 1789 (Archives nationales); see liminalweb and Wikipedia 'Storming of the Bastille'

entries.headline: A bookseller records alarm bells, arms hunts and the fortress's fall
entries.digest: Hardy logs the day as rumours reach him: crowds searching for arms and powder, the alarm bell, the attack on the Bastille, and the killing of its governor de Launay and of the merchants' provost Flesselles. As always he writes what 'comes to his knowledge', mixing what he saw with what he heard.
entries.source_note: Hardy, Mes loisirs, July 1789 (Bastien et al. edition); contents summarised from secondary literature, not checked against the edition

entries.headline: Two heads on pikes in a cheering crowd
entries.digest: Rigby is among the crowds when the news of victory spreads. He sees two bloody heads held up on pikes, said to be those of de Launay, the Bastille's governor, and Flesselles, the merchants' provost, and records his revulsion amid the general joy. He had been cheering the people's courage minutes before.
entries.source_note: Dr. Rigby's Letters from France &c. in 1789 (1880), cited in Wikipedia 'Storming of the Bastille'; the date of the letter itself was not checked

entries.headline: Touring the cells of a fortress two days fallen
entries.digest: Morris goes to see the Bastille, already a tourist site where the demolition crews have started work, and walks through its cells. He views it with curiosity and keeps his skepticism about the people who took it.
entries.source_note: Preface to Journal de Gouverneur Morris (Plon 1901) mentions his visit to the Bastille cells on 16 July; the diary text itself was not checked

entries.headline: A minister's dispatch: the Bastille, the militia, the king's surrender
entries.digest: Jefferson sends Foreign Secretary John Jay a long, step-by-step account of the week: the troops ringing the city, Necker's dismissal, the arms seized at the Invalides, the taking of the Bastille, and the king's visit to Paris to accept the new order. He writes as a sympathiser who believes the crisis is ending.
entries.source_note: Jefferson to John Jay, 19 July 1789 (Papers of Thomas Jefferson); cited by Wikipedia 'Storming of the Bastille'; the date is from memory and was not checked in this session

entries.headline: Watching a mob gut Strasbourg's town hall
entries.digest: Young is passing through Strasbourg when a crowd storms and loots the town hall. They throw papers and furniture from the windows while the troops look on. He records how the revolution of Paris reached a provincial city as a riot over bread and municipal grievances.
entries.source_note: Archives d'Alsace, 'fiche pillage 20 juillet 1789' (notes Young's presence that day); Travels in France

entries.headline: Foulon's head arrives in triumph while Morris waits for his carriage
entries.digest: After dinner Morris is strolling under the Palais-Royal arcade when a crowd brings in the head of the old minister Foulon on a pike, with the naked body dragged behind. He then learns that the remains were shown to Foulon's son-in-law, the intendant Bertier, who was killed and cut to pieces in turn. He notes Foulon's 'crime': accepting a place in the ministry. The entry ends with a cry of disgust at the cruelty of the people.
entries.source_note: Diary, 22 July 1789 (Diary and Letters, 1888). Not read directly here: the passage under the Palais-Royal arcade, waiting for a carriage, appears in English at revolution.chnm.org/d/384, where it is credited to the Duchesse de Gontaut and dated 14 July. Its wording and details fit Morris's diary for 22 July.

entries.headline: The lantern, the hay in the mouth, the son-in-law
entries.digest: Hardy records the arrest of Foulon, who had been rumoured to say the hungry could eat grass, his hanging from the lamp-post at the Grève when the rope broke, and his head paraded with hay in its mouth. Bertier was brought in from Compiègne the same evening and killed. The bookseller's horror is mixed with a sense that the crowd felt it was doing justice.
entries.source_note: Hardy, Mes loisirs, 22 July 1789; summarised from secondary literature

entries.headline: Telling Madison the whole revolution in one letter
entries.digest: Jefferson tells Madison the story from the royal session of 23 June, through the troop build-up and the fall of the Bastille, to the king's return of Necker. In a postscript he adds that Foulon has been seized and killed by the mob and that Bertier is reported massacred. He presents the killings as an afterword to a victory.
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Madison, 22 July 1789, Founders Online

entries.headline: Foulon and Bertier, then a note about money
entries.digest: Writing to Thomas Paine, Jefferson describes Foulon dragged through the main streets headless and Bertier killed on arrival. He hopes the violence will stop, since only the capture of other hated men could restart it. He then turns to Paine's money troubles and mentions that Gouverneur Morris leaves for London in a few days.
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Paine, 23 July 1789, Founders Online

entries.headline: The news of Paris reaches a royalist ambassador
entries.digest: In Venice, Bombelles receives by courier the news of the Bastille, the king's capitulation in Paris and the first emigrations. He takes it as a catastrophe for throne and altar and as a personal grief for the royal family his wife serves.
entries.source_note: Journal du marquis de Bombelles (Droz edition), July 1789; exact entry not checked

entries.headline: Châteaux burning, and an Englishman made to wear a cockade
entries.digest: Riding south, Young passes through country where peasants have attacked and burned châteaux and seized the lords' papers (the Great Fear). Villagers stop him for not wearing the tricolour cockade, and he has to talk his way past suspicion that he is an agent of the aristocrats. The traveller has become a suspect.
entries.source_note: Travels in France, late July 1789 entries; exact day not checked

entries.place: Châtillon woods near Meudon, then Versailles
entries.headline: Shooting interrupted: the women reach Versailles
entries.digest: Louis is out shooting at the Porte de Châtillon and logs his bag as usual, 81 head of game. He notes that the day was interrupted by 'events' and that he rode out and back. Those events were thousands of Parisian women, then Lafayette's National Guard, marching on Versailles over bread.
entries.source_note: Journal of Louis XVI, 5 October 1789 (Nicolardot edition); widely cited, but not checked in this session

entries.headline: The market women march out in the rain
entries.digest: Hardy records the women of the Halles and the faubourgs gathering at the Hôtel de Ville over the price and shortage of bread, dragging cannon and marching off toward Versailles. The National Guard follows them by evening. He notes the rumours of an insult to the cockade at a royal banquet that had inflamed the city.
entries.source_note: Hardy, Mes loisirs, 5 October 1789; summarised from secondary literature

entries.headline: The king's terse log of leaving Versailles forever
entries.digest: The journal notes a departure for Paris after noon, a visit to the Hôtel de Ville, then supper and bed at the Tuileries. It gives no hint of the dawn invasion of the palace, the murdered bodyguards, or the crowd escorting the 'baker, baker's wife and baker's boy'. It is the same flat style as a hunting day.
entries.source_note: Journal of Louis XVI, 6 October 1789; widely cited, not checked in this session

entries.headline: Heads on pikes ahead of the royal carriage
entries.digest: Hardy hears that the crowd broke into the palace at dawn, and he records the long procession that evening bringing the royal family into Paris, with bread wagons and the heads of slain guards carried ahead. Within weeks his 36-year journal stops, as if the city he chronicled had ended.
entries.source_note: Hardy, Mes loisirs, 6 October 1789; journal ends October 1789 (Wikipedia)

entries.headline: The Federation: a revolution as a festival
entries.digest: Williams, newly arrived from London, watches the Festival of the Federation: a vast earthwork amphitheatre that Parisians of every class had dug by hand, the oath at the altar of the nation, and rain that did not dampen the crowd. She writes that she has seen the triumph of human liberty and that her heart was won.
entries.source_note: Letters Written in France (1790), letter on the Federation; dates of her letters are loose

entries.headline: Why she will not follow her aunts abroad
entries.digest: As her elderly aunts leave for Rome, Élisabeth explains in a letter that she does not believe her duty calls her to emigrate. She will stay beside her brother, a decision that will take her to the Temple and the scaffold.
entries.source_note: Letter of February 1791 (cited in Wikipedia, Élisabeth of France)

entries.headline: Woken at night, dressed as someone else
entries.digest: Marie-Thérèse later remembered being woken and disguised. Her small brother was dressed as a girl, and the governess Madame de Tourzel posed as a Russian baroness, while the family slipped out of the Tuileries around midnight. The child understood only that they were going somewhere secret.
entries.source_note: Her account of the flight to Varennes (later memoir; Alpha History); the departure time is confirmed by Wikipedia 'Flight to Varennes'

entries.headline: A journey logged like a hunt: left at midnight, arrested at eleven
entries.digest: The king's journal records the flight in two clauses: departure from Paris at midnight, and arrival and arrest at Varennes at eleven in the evening. Postmaster Drouet had recognised him at Sainte-Menehould. The disaster that destroyed his credibility reads like an itinerary.
entries.source_note: Journal of Louis XVI, 21 June 1791; widely cited, not checked in this session

entries.headline: An anecdote of the king's childhood cruelty
entries.digest: On the second anniversary of the Bastille, three weeks after Varennes, Morris hears a story of Louis's cruelty to animals as a boy. He writes in disgust that it is no wonder such a creature is being dethroned. The admirer of 1789 has turned contemptuous.
entries.source_note: Journal de Gouverneur Morris (Plon 1901), preface citing the entry of 14 July 1791

entries.headline: The absurd return with Barnave and Pétion
entries.digest: Writing to Angélique de Bombelles, Élisabeth describes the slow, humiliating return from Varennes squeezed in the coach with the Assembly's deputies Barnave and Pétion. With dark humour she calls the scene ridiculous. Barnave's courtesy to the queen on that ride would later help convict him.
entries.source_note: Letter to Mme de Bombelles on the Varennes journey (Wikipedia, Élisabeth of France); exact date not checked

entries.headline: France like cattle before a storm
entries.digest: A week after presenting his credentials to Louis XVI, Morris reports to Jefferson: war with Austria going badly, an undisciplined army, paper money out of control, the cabinet split. He warns that a nation this exhausted may accept despotism for the sake of quiet.
entries.source_note: Morris to Jefferson, 10 June 1792, Founders Online (Jefferson/01-24-02-0049)

entries.headline: A republican mother hears the cannon at the Tuileries
entries.digest: Rosalie Jullien writes to her husband as the faubourgs and the fédérés storm the Tuileries and the Swiss Guards fall. She describes the gunfire, the tocsin and the bodies, and she rejoices that the 'tyrant' has been overthrown. Her enthusiasm is the counterpoint to the royal family's terror that same morning.
entries.source_note: Lockroy (ed.), Journal d'une bourgeoise pendant la Révolution (1881); L. Parker, Writing the Revolution (2013); exact letter date not checked

entries.headline: Leaving the palace for the last time
entries.digest: Marie-Thérèse remembered the family leaving the Tuileries early in the morning, crossing the garden to take refuge with the Legislative Assembly, and spending hours crammed into the cramped reporters' box while fighting raged at the palace behind them. The monarchy was suspended before evening.
entries.source_note: Her later memoir; the event and date are confirmed by Wikipedia 'Insurrection of 10 August 1792'

entries.headline: The family enters the Temple
entries.digest: Cléry records the royal family's transfer to the Temple, first to the small tower and then to the great tower, where he would serve the king. He describes the bare rooms, the guards' insults, and the family's attempt to keep a daily routine of lessons and meals.
entries.source_note: Cléry, Journal (London 1798); the Temple date is confirmed by Wikipedia 'Marie-Thérèse of France'; when Cléry himself arrived was not checked

entries.headline: Business as usual, a week after the monarchy fell
entries.digest: A week after the Tuileries massacre, Morris's official letter to Jefferson deals with foreign officers' pay certificates, Kosciuszko's claim on the United States, and a squabble over the vice-consulship at Dunkirk. The paperwork of a small republic carries on through the collapse of a great monarchy.
entries.source_note: Morris to Jefferson, 17 August 1792, Founders Online (Jefferson/01-24-02-0289)

entries.headline: His house searched; Saint-Domingue's debt; staying on
entries.digest: Morris refuses to sign a contract with the new ministers for money to relieve Saint-Domingue, which is burning in a slave revolt, saying he has no authority to deal with them. Section commissioners search his house for hidden arms on an informer's word, and he sends them off. The British ambassador has gone, but Morris stays.
entries.source_note: Morris to Jefferson, 30 August 1792, Founders Online (Jefferson/01-24-02-0312)

entries.headline: A night-walker at the prison gates
entries.digest: Restif describes wandering through the September nights as the prisons were emptied by summary 'tribunals' and the prisoners butchered. He claims to have seen the Princesse de Lamballe, the queen's friend, dragged out and killed, and her body mutilated. He writes as a horrified witness, in prose that is clearly literary.
entries.source_note: Les Nuits de Paris (Alpha History excerpt, 'Retif describes the September Massacres'); Lamballe was killed on 3 September; Restif's genre is flagged

entries.headline: An ambassador's tally of the September killings
entries.digest: Morris reports that the killing began on the afternoon of the 2nd and went on about a week, with perhaps thousands dead. Among them were hundreds of non-juring priests, the Abbaye prisoners, Madame de Lamballe, the Duc de La Rochefoucauld murdered under escort, and his old acquaintance Montmorin. He notes that there is no real executive left to stop it.
entries.source_note: Morris to Jefferson, 10 September 1792, Founders Online (Jefferson/01-24-02-0335)

entries.place: her lodgings in the Marais, Paris
entries.headline: The king rides past to his trial
entries.digest: From her window Wollstonecraft watches Louis driven to the Convention to hear his defence. The streets are silent and lined with National Guards. She is surprised to find herself in tears at his dignity, and alone that night she is frightened by her own imagination.
entries.source_note: Letter to Joseph Johnson, 26 December 1792, Posthumous Works (1798); not re-checked in this session

entries.headline: The king's fate: he must die or reign
entries.digest: Writing privately to Washington, Morris passes on the king's own reckoning: if the Convention refers his case to the people, he expects a mob to kill him. Morris's view is blunter. Five days earlier his diary had fallen silent, and it would stay silent until October 1794.
entries.source_note: Morris to Washington, 10 January 1793, Founders Online; the diary gap (5 Jan 1793–12 Oct 1794) is from the LOC finding aid

entries.headline: The last meeting with the family
entries.digest: Cléry describes the evening the king was allowed to see his wife, sister and children for the last time, in the dining room behind a glass door that the guards watched. He tells of the weeping, the promise to see them in the morning, and the king's decision to spare them a second farewell.
entries.source_note: Cléry, Journal (1798); memoir-like text

entries.headline: A daughter's last evening with her father
entries.digest: Marie-Thérèse remembered her father's calm and the family's grief, and that he told the children to forgive his killers. She remembered fainting at the end, and that he did not come in the morning as promised.
entries.source_note: Memoir of the captivity in the Temple (written about 1795)

entries.headline: Waking the king for the last time
entries.digest: Cléry wakes Louis at five, dresses him, and serves the Mass that Edgeworth says in the room. The king hands him small keepsakes for the queen and the children. Cléry is not allowed to go with him, and he hears the drums carry the carriage away.
entries.source_note: Cléry, Journal (1798); the details are confirmed by Wikipedia 'Execution of Louis XVI'

entries.headline: On the scaffold steps
entries.digest: Edgeworth rides with the king to the Place de la Révolution and persuades him to let his hands be tied. He climbs the scaffold beside him and sees Louis try to speak to the crowd before Santerre's drums drown him out. He kneels as the blade falls. The famous blessing attributed to him is a tradition he never confirmed.
entries.source_note: Edgeworth, Memoirs (1815); the time and details are from Wikipedia 'Execution of Louis XVI'

entries.headline: A bookseller's quiet dread after the execution
entries.digest: Ruault writes to his brother about the execution and how the city took it: shops shut, the streets watched, some people dipping cloths in the blood, most people silent. He is a patriot, but he is no longer sure where the Revolution is going.
entries.source_note: Gazette d'un Parisien sous la Révolution (1976); the date and content of this letter were not checked

entries.headline: A letter on the 'present character' of the French
entries.digest: In an open letter to Johnson, Wollstonecraft sets out to judge the French nation and admits that her hopes are under strain. She sees vanity, theatricality and bloodshed where she expected virtue, but she still insists that the old regime made them so. It is a radical's first doubts, written three weeks after the king's death.
entries.source_note: 'Letter on the Present Character of the French Nation', dated 15 February 1793, Posthumous Works (1798)

entries.headline: An English admirer of the Revolution arrested
entries.digest: When the Convention orders the arrest of British subjects, Williams and her mother and sister are taken into custody and spend weeks in prison. She later wrote of fellow prisoners, Girondins and their friends among them, going one by one to the tribunal. The enthusiast of 1790 now sees the Revolution from inside its prisons.
entries.source_note: Letters from France (later series); the month is approximate

entries.headline: The queen's last letter, to Élisabeth
entries.digest: Hours after her conviction, the queen writes to her sister-in-law that she is innocent, at peace with God, and anxious for her children, and she asks Élisabeth to tell her son never to avenge them. She was guillotined at about a quarter past noon. The letter never reached Élisabeth, who was executed in May 1794.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia 'Marie Antoinette' (last letter and execution time)

entries.headline: Looking back on the Terror from Hamburg
entries.digest: Finally out of France, Morris tells Washington what he could not write down: daily misery he could do nothing about, the humiliation of dealing with 'the worst of mankind', and a woman arrested in his own house by the Committee of General Safety. He predicts the Revolution will end in a single despotism. His diary resumed only after he left Paris.
entries.source_note: Morris to Washington, 30 December 1794, Founders Online (Washington/05-17-02-0231)

convergences.label: Fall of the Bastille
convergences.note: The king's log has nothing; the bookseller lists rumours; the English doctor sees the heads go by. The same day reads as an empty page, a chronicle and a trauma.

convergences.label: Lynching of Foulon and Bertier
convergences.note: Morris, a few yards away, is horrified; Hardy reports it as the people's justice gone wild; Jefferson, writing the same night, treats it as a postscript to a victory. It shows how distance and politics shape a description.

convergences.label: The women's march on Versailles
convergences.note: Louis logs 81 head of game and an 'interruption'; Hardy logs the women leaving Paris with cannon. Two pages written the same day show the gap that the march itself closed.

convergences.label: Flight to Varennes
convergences.note: Three members of one family in one coach: the king's itinerary, the child's memory of disguises, and the sister's sardonic letter about the return.

convergences.label: Fall of the monarchy
convergences.note: The republican mother cheers, the princess hides in the reporters' box, and a week later the American minister files routine paperwork.

convergences.label: Execution of Louis XVI
convergences.note: The servant in the tower, the priest on the scaffold, the daughter left behind and the bookseller in the street, while the best-placed foreign diarist in Paris writes nothing: Morris's diary is silent from 5 January.

ties.note: Close friends and fellow Americans in Paris. They had silhouettes made together at the Palais-Royal on 22 April 1789, and Jefferson mentions Morris in his letter of 23 July.
Morris was presented to Louis XVI as US Minister on 3 June 1792 and later helped plan an escape attempt for him.
Élisabeth's chief correspondent was Angélique de Bombelles, the ambassador's wife, so letters from the Tuileries fed his journal.
The queen's last letter was addressed to her sister-in-law, who never received it.
Father and daughter, writing about the same coach at Varennes and the same farewell in the Temple.
Both attended the king on the morning of 21 January 1793. Cléry served the Mass that Edgeworth said.
Both were in the British radical circle in Paris in 1793, and Wollstonecraft visited Williams's salon.
Both were Paris booksellers of the Latin Quarter trade; Ruault's letters continue where Hardy's journal stops.
On 10 August 1792 one cheers the overthrow while the other hides from it in the Assembly.

threads_out.note: The Revolution's armies became Napoleon's. The émigré nobles of 1789 to 1792 turned up in Russian service, and the Grande Armée that entered Moscow descended from the levée of 1793.

Jefferson, the Paris witness of 1789, wrote the Declaration whose promises the Civil War fought over. Morris's 1792 letters on aid to Saint-Domingue touch the Haitian Revolution, which frightened American slaveholders for decades.
The Bolsheviks read their revolution through the French one: Jacobins, Terror, and fear of a 'Thermidor' shaped Lenin's and Trotsky's debates.
The guillotine, the metric system, the citizen army and the very words 'left' and 'right' run from 1789 through every later chapter.
